meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'брый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('kind; good').

examples.trans: Good evening!
She is very kind.

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'day' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Good afternoon!
I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning '(emphasis) after all, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.
But you've still got some.
I told you: no.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'seemingly, like, apparently', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything seems completely fine.
Seems not, we are not rushing.
He seems to take it fine.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

перейти.gloss: to cross, switch, move on to

meanings.en: to cross, switch, move on to
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to cross, switch, move on to', paired with 'переходить'.

examples.text: А теперь перейдём к другим новостям.
examples.trans: And now let us move on to other news.
They crossed the road.

examples.text: А теперь перешли к другим новостям.
examples.trans: And now they moved on to other news.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'казаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to seem, appear', paired with 'казаться'.

examples.text: Тебе показалось, она смотрела на всех.
examples.trans: You imagined it, she was looking at everyone.
I wanted to show it to the local policeman.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'yesterday', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Yesterday I was at home.
Yesterday was Friday.

examples.text: Я вчера ел маринованные грибы. Может, один гриб был плохой.
examples.trans: Yesterday I ate pickled mushrooms. Maybe one mushroom was bad.

meanings.note: Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'статься'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to break up, to part', paired with 'расставаться'.

examples.trans: We will definitely break up.
They broke up last summer.

examples.text: Нет, я всё решил! Мы с ней точно расстанемся.
examples.trans: No, I have decided everything! She and I will definitely break up.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
How are you? — OK.
Good! Everything's fine over there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'after all, you know', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I did tell you, you know!

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

examples.text: Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'certainly', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Поймите, была маленькая ошибка. Вы уж нас извините.
examples.trans: Understand, there was a small mistake. Please forgive us.
Indeed, not very well at all.
Certainly much better than you!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: From German 'Konkurrent' / Latin 'concurrens' ('running together', rival).

examples.trans: Who are your rivals?
He has no rivals.
Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to fight, struggle', paired with 'побороться'.

examples.trans: We must fight for victory.
He is struggling with his doubts.
Alright, keep fighting for power.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I was only looking.
Just one.
I was only looking!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to think', paired with 'подумать'.

examples.trans: I'm thinking about work.
I have no time to think about that.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to live'.

examples.trans: I live in a communal flat.
I want to live normally.

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('left').

examples.text: Вот у меня на левой руке золотые часы!
examples.trans: Here on my left hand I have a gold watch!
Turn to the left side of the street.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'which, who', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Чтобы он вернул деньги, которые украл.
examples.trans: For him to give back the money he stole.

examples.text: Который ему город подарил! И откуда у Аллы Евгеньевны новая шуба!
examples.trans: Which the city donated to him! And where Alla Yevgenyevna got a new fur coat!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'mum, mother' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Mum, where's my phone?
My mum is a doctor.
Mum, what's a bidet?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'uh-huh, yeah', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Uh-huh, I see.
Yeah, right!
Yeah, right, like with the Cayenne?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

снять.gloss: to film, to photograph; to take off; to rent

meanings.en: to film, to photograph; to take off; to rent
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'нять'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to film, to photograph; to take off; to rent', paired with 'снимать'.

examples.text: Я сняла пьяного соседа на телефон.
examples.trans: I filmed a drunk neighbour on my phone.
He took off his coat by the door.

examples.text: Я сняла пьяного соседа на телефон. И сразу все мне помогают!
examples.trans: I filmed a drunk neighbour on my phone. And right away everyone helps me!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to play', paired with 'сыграть'.

examples.text: Напиши: трус не играет в хоккей.
examples.trans: Write: a coward doesn't play hockey.
The children are playing in the courtyard.

examples.text: Хорошая фотография! Напиши: трус не играет в хоккей.
examples.trans: Good photo! Write: a coward doesn't play hockey.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in (time); through', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'll come in an hour.
In a week.

examples.text: Нормально? Она через неделю снова потечёт!
examples.trans: Fine? It'll be leaking again in a week!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'time, occasion' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Just once.
Say it once more.
What do you mean, once?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'more; still; yet', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to say, to tell', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: What did you say?
Excuse me, where's the metro?
Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'car; machine' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Is this our car now?
Which car did you come in?
A car. A German one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how; as', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How was it in Hungary?
As you all know...
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'росток'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'teenager, adolescent' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: You are behaving like a teenager!
The teenagers were walking in the courtyard.

examples.text: Вы ведёте себя как подросток! Вы приударяете за мной.
examples.trans: You are behaving like a teenager! You are flirting with me.
